title: The campaign, end to end
summary: A guided pass over the whole of 1914 in the West: the timetable, Liège, the Frontiers, the retreat, the wheel inside Paris, the Marne, and the line that followed. It stops at the four decisions the campaign turned on, and shows the counterfactual once.

steps.title: A plan is a bet about time
steps.narration:
Germany went to war in the West with a plan that was really a timetable: beat France in about six weeks, then turn east before Russia was ready.[^herwig-2009] Everything you are about to watch is that bet being settled — not by one decision, but by distance, railways, Belgian forts and the choices of the other side.[^strachan-2001]

What the plan actually was is itself contested: an operational plan Moltke inherited and diluted, or a memorandum turned into a legend after the war.[^zuber-2002] Both readings are in the dossier.

steps.title: Two clocks start together
steps.narration:
On 4 August the German armies cross into Belgium and the campaign clock starts. Beside it runs the plan's own clock — the days the timetable expected to need — and the Russian mobilization it was racing.[^mombauer-2001]

Seven armies deployed in the West, one in the East: the whole bet in one number.[^herwig-2009] Watch the gauge under the timeline as the days pass; the gap between the two clocks is the story.

steps.title: Liège: eleven days the plan did not have
steps.narration:
The road west runs through Liège, and Liège is a ring of twelve forts. The city falls on 7 August; the forts hold until 16 August, and only super-heavy siege artillery ends them.[^herwig-2009]

The delay is smaller than the legend and larger than the timetable could afford — and every day of it is a day the French and British get to concentrate.[^strachan-2001]

steps.title: Plan XVII walks into the trap
steps.narration:
While the wheel swings through Belgium, the French attack where the plan wanted them to: east, into Lorraine. On 20 August the offensive breaks at Morhange and Sarrebourg.[^afgg-1-1]

The German success here is a problem for Germany. Rupprecht's counter-attack pulls strength toward the hinge and hands the French an army they can move somewhere else.[^herwig-2009]

steps.title: 22 August
steps.narration:
The bloodiest day in French history: on this single day, in the Ardennes and on the Sambre, roughly 27,000 French soldiers are killed.[^steg-2013] It is not a battle anyone planned — armies collide in fog and standing corn.

The card holds what is known and how firmly. Nothing here is a score.

steps.title: Charleroi, Mons, and the order to fall back
steps.narration:
On the Sambre and at Mons the French Fifth Army and the British Expeditionary Force meet the right wing head-on, and both give ground.[^edmonds-1922] Joffre orders a general retreat rather than a stand.

The wing is winning every encounter and still not catching anyone. That is the shape of the next fortnight.[^tyng-1935]

steps.title: Decision: two corps for East Prussia
steps.narration:
25 August. With Russian armies in East Prussia, Moltke detaches the Guard Reserve Corps and XI Corps from the decisive wing and entrains them east.[^reichsarchiv-weltkrieg-1]

They arrive too late for Tannenberg and are absent at the Marne — the clearest single case of the timetable being paid for twice.[^mombauer-2001] Read the options, then let the tour move on.

steps.title: Where the right wing bleeds
steps.narration:
East Prussia is not the only debt. Antwerp has to be masked, Namur and Maubeuge besieged, lines of communication guarded — each takes corps out of the wheel.[^herwig-2009]

The ledger beside the clock counts what leaves. By the Marne the outer wing is markedly weaker than the plan assumed.[^strachan-2001]

steps.title: Rail against feet
steps.narration:
The Germans advance at the speed of boots and horses while their railheads crawl forward behind blown Belgian tunnels and bridges. The French fall back onto their own intact network — and Joffre uses it, moving whole corps west by train to build a new army near Paris.[^herwig-2009]

The gauge reads the gap between an army and its railhead. Beyond a few marches, supply stops being a line on a map.[^strachan-2001]

steps.title: Decision: wheel inside Paris
steps.narration:
30–31 August. Kluck turns his First Army south-east, inside Paris rather than around it, to keep contact with Bülow and finish the French Fifth Army.[^kluck-1920]

It is defensible on the information he had — and it exposes his flank to a city he has stopped watching.[^tyng-1935]

steps.title: The other story: if the wheel had stayed wide
steps.narration:
Here is the counterfactual, labelled as one. Schlieffen's concept branch keeps the weight on the outer wing and swings west of Paris — the sweep the memorandum described.[^zuber-2002]

Watch the tokens take the wider arc, then ask the feasibility checklist what would have had to be true: more corps, more supply, more days than the marching had left.[^herwig-2009]

steps.title: Decision: halt and face Paris
steps.narration:
Back on the historical branch. On 4 September the German command finally sees the threat gathering out of Paris and orders the right wing to turn and face it.[^reichsarchiv-weltkrieg-1]

The order is right and late: turning First Army to meet Maunoury opens a gap between it and Bülow.[^tyng-1935]

steps.title: The gap, and the Marne
steps.narration:
5 September: the French Sixth Army strikes east out of Paris toward the Ourcq, and Kluck feeds his corps back north-west to meet it.[^gallieni-1920] The gap between the two German armies widens to some fifty kilometres, and the BEF and the French Fifth Army walk into it.[^edmonds-1922]

No one is being destroyed here. Something simpler is happening: the plan is running out of time.

steps.title: Decision: authorize the retreat
steps.narration:
9 September, late morning. Lieutenant-Colonel Hentsch arrives at First Army headquarters with the authority of a supreme command 200 kilometres away, and the German right wing is ordered back.[^kluck-1920]

What exactly he was empowered to do has been argued over ever since — the army that lost wanted a reason, and a staff officer made a convenient one.[^herwig-2009]

steps.title: The line that stayed
steps.narration:
The Germans fall back to the Aisne heights and dig in; the attacks that follow fail, and both sides begin reaching north for an open flank that is closing.[^edmonds-1922]

The bet is settled. The war of movement ends in a line of trenches, and the plan's six weeks become four years.[^strachan-2001]
